issues.title: HTTP/1.1 do not support multiplexing at all…
issues.author: philsbln
issues.body:
While the argument in Section 2 "requests are strictly serialised in the connection, therefore demultiplexing is not needed" is technically correct, Section 4. further restricts the use of HTTP/1.1 connections to a single stream of capsules/HTTP datagrams. 

I would prefer to see this restriction as an argument here.

issues.title: Is the Capsule Protocol a premature abstraction?
issues.author: mnot
issues.body:
This protocol is being introduced with one use case, and that case is a generalisation that's capable of incorporating almost anything (datagrams). 

Is this a case of premature abstraction?

While from an implementation standpoint this abstraction might not be expensive, adding a new abstraction to HTTP's core data model isn't something we should do lightly; the road is littered with failed and poorly-integrated attempts.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body:
At the MASQUE Interim in April 2021, the WG reached consensus on strongly associating HTTP Datagrams with requests, and the fact that HTTP Datagrams would work across intermediaries. We also established that there was a need to register context semantics end-to-end.  That same day, Ben Schwartz proposed the name capsule for such a system and we've kept it since. In the past year, we've thoroughly discussed capsules among the Working Group, and the possibility of premature optimization was discussed. The Working Group decided that this was a useful abstraction, and CONNECT-IP and WebTransport both started using the abstraction, confirming that it was useful. The final design of the Capsule Protocol came out of the HTTP Datagrams design team, was presented at the February 2022 MASQUE Interim and Working Group consensus was declared by the chairs [on the mailing list last month](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/masque/GXaxmCJoo122ymqyAqTUaUFix_k/).

Unless you have any new information that would warrant revisiting this consensus, I'd suggest closing this issue with no action.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: Closing this based on the comment above since today marks the end of WGLC

issues.title: Consider rephrasing H3_DATAGRAM setting text
issues.author: LPardue
issues.body: The current text talks about "supporting" HTTP/3 datagrams. It seems we could tighten this up to be more about the willingness to receive datagrams a la https://httpwg.org/http2-spec/draft-ietf-httpbis-http2bis.html#section-6.5.2

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: SGTM

issues.title: Clarify sentence
issues.author: mirjak
issues.body:
End of section 3.3. (error handing) says:

`When a stream carrying capsules terminates cleanly, if the last capsule on the stream was truncated, this MUST be treated as a malformed or incomplete message.`

 Not sure I can parse that sentence correctly. Is that

`When a stream carrying capsules terminates cleanly BUT the last capsule on the stream was truncated, this MUST be treated as a malformed or incomplete message.`

?

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
"terminates cleanly" is an abstract way of covering all HTTP versions notion of a stream FIN. This is not well defined (maybe lost in one of the restructuring edits?).

If we think of HTTP/3 and the request stream being FIN'd at a particular offset, that is independent of a parser acting on the data in the stream.

I think the way to make this clearer is to define or reference stream closures in respective HTTP docs.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: How about this? `When a stream carrying capsules terminates cleanly (for example, in HTTP/3 this is defined as receiving a QUIC STREAM frame with the FIN bit set), if the last capsule on the stream was truncated, this MUST be treated as a malformed or incomplete message.`

comments.author: mirjak
comments.body:
I don't understand the sentence structure here: When ..., if ..., then. Why is there a when and an if with a comma? May this should be: When ... and if ..., then?

Sorry if that is grammatically correct but it really confuses me what the sentence is supposed to say...

P.S.: clarifying the term "terminates cleanly" is also a good idea though.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: We could rephrase as `If a stream carrying capsules terminates cleanly (for example, in HTTP/3 this is defined as receiving a QUIC STREAM frame with the FIN bit set) and the last capsule on the stream was truncated, this MUST be treated as a malformed or incomplete message.` How does that sound?

comments.author: mirjak
comments.body: Yes, that works for me. Thanks!

issues.title: Paragraph on use of capsule protocol and http datagrams is unclear
issues.author: mirjak
issues.body:
End of section 3.5 ([The DATAGRAM Capsule](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-masque-h3-datagram-08.html#name-the-datagram-capsule)) says:

```
Note that use of the Capsule Protocol is not required to use HTTP Datagrams. 
If an HTTP extension that uses HTTP Datagrams is only defined over transports
that support QUIC DATAGRAM frames, it might not need a stream encoding.
Additionally, HTTP extensions can use HTTP Datagrams with their own data
stream protocol. However, new HTTP extensions that wish to use HTTP Datagrams
SHOULD use the Capsule Protocol unless they have a good reason not to.
```

First of all this paragraph seems to be in the wrong section because it's more generally about the capsule protocol and not the datagram capsule.

However, it's also confusing. I believe if you negotiate http datagram with the H3_DATAGRAM SETTINGS parameter, you always need to also support capsules even if QUIC datagrams are supported, as the other end (e.g. an intermediary) could send you anyway a capsule.

Or is this text meant to say that new extensions that use the http datagram but have a new settings parameter for negotiation may not need to support the capsule protocol?

I think it would be good to clarify both: what this sentence/paragraph means and what is required if you negotiate http datagrams using the H3_DATAGRAM SETTINGS parameter.

comments.author: gloinul
comments.body:
I want to extended on this issue a bit more. A lot about the implementation requirement on different nodes are implied rather than being explicit. 

"Secondly, I will note that the above text combined with what is written in Section 3.4:
Intermediaries MAY use this header field to allow processing of HTTP Datagrams for unknown HTTP Upgrade Tokens; note that this is only possible for HTTP Upgrade or Extended CONNECT."

If an intermediary is doing this unaware re-encoding and the HTTP extension is an extended connect version it can result in interoperability failure when a Datagram capsule arrives at the endpoint that only supports HTTP/3 Datagrams over QUIC Datagram.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
If we build off the notion that H3_DATAGRAM setting communicates a willingness to receive the HTTP/3 datagrams (in QUIC datagrams), they still require some request to bootstrap the association, otherwise those datagrams would be ignored. 

In theory, I could define a new method called "ALWAYS_UNRELIABLE" that can be used to bootstrap a request stream and it be defined to never use a capsule protocol. If a server sends me data on that stream, I could ignore it or throw an error. I don't need a new setting to caveat this behaviour.

comments.author: gloinul
comments.body: @LPardue but then you can't have "blind" re-encoding of HTTP/3 Datagram to Datagram capsules, I think it is that simple. So we need to choose if HTTP Intermediaries can re-encode when they don't know the Upgrade Token or if they can't and must be aware and thus enable cases where some have different behaviors. See #168

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: There is no such thing as "blind re-encoding". Intermediaries can only perform re-encoding when they know that the capsule protocol is in use. Intermediaries can learn that by knowing the HTTP Upgrade Token, or by watching for the Capsule-Protocol header. But I think we can make that clearer by spelling out in the "DATAGRAM Capsule" section that intermediaries MUST NOT re-encode to capsules unless they know for sure that the capsule protocol is in use.

comments.author: mirjak
comments.body: PR #168 did not address the editorial point that this paragraph is in the wrong section.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: I don't agree with that editorial point. The paragraph is about the interaction between HTTP datagrams and the capsule protocol, so having in the DATAGRAM capsule section makes sense to me.

comments.author: mirjak
comments.body: It about the interaction about http datagrams (section 2) and the capsule protocol (section 3). There is nothing related to datagram capsules (section 3.5) in this paragraph. I guess you could just add a new subsection 3.6 if you prefer to have it at the end.

issues.title: SHOULD or MUST intermediaries forward unknown capsule types without modification?
issues.author: mirjak
issues.body:
The first SHOULD should be a MUST because there is a clear exception specified but in all other cases this is a MUST.

The second SHOULD should really be a MUST. Or why is that a SHOULD?
If there is a reason for a SHOULD this needs to be explained but I think it would break interoperability.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: I personally preferred MUST, however the consensus of the design team was SHOULD, and that was confirmed by the WG. Let's no reopen that unless we have new information.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body:
On #166, @mirjak said:
> I definitely missed this nuance during the wg call. What's the reason for a should?

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: I think the main motivation was that the MUST was unenforceable, and that there will be intermediaries that explicitly want to block unknown extensions for security reasons.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Whatever we might prefer, isn't this a case where whatever the specification says, intermediaries will do what they want?

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: I agree. That's why in the interest of making progress I'd rather move forward with the design team consensus instead of reopening this topic.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
design team outputs don't have any special status here; perhaps the answer is not to say "SHOULD this" or "MUST that" but to instead articulate the intent behind the design and the potential consequences of not complying with that intent.

Perhaps the key reason for mandating forwarding is that the meaning of various protocol elements is only valid in the context of all of the messages that an endpoint says.  That is, you might send a bunch of datagram capsules that have meaning derived from other capsules.  Remove the other capsules and you change the meaning of those datagram capsules.  An intermediary that adds, modifies, or removes any capsules needs to understand the totality of the effect of their interventions.

This is why I remain skeptical about the value of the generic capsule protocol.  It only has value if it can be acted upon generically, but it is not obvious that it can be.  Put differently, the existence of a generic capsule protocol implies a number of constraints on the operation of extensions that are not obvious and not clearly articulated.

@gloinul might be asking about similar effects in #168.

comments.author: gloinul
comments.body:
So lets start with explaining the interoperability issue that is at the core of this:

So the draft currently has several statements that interact with each other to cause this interoperability issue. 

Section 3.5 says: 

'Note that use of the Capsule Protocol is not required to use HTTP Datagrams. If an HTTP extension that uses HTTP Datagrams is only defined over transports that support QUIC DATAGRAM frames, it might not need a stream encoding.'

Section 3.5 also says: 

'An intermediary can reencode HTTP Datagrams as it forwards them. In other words, an intermediary MAY send a DATAGRAM capsule to forward an HTTP Datagram which was received in a QUIC DATAGRAM frame, and vice versa.'

Thus the following may occur:

Endpoint 1 sends a HTTP datagram as HTTP/3 Datagram over QUIC datagram. The HTTP intermediary re-encode this blind of its context to an Capsule Datagram and forward it to another HTTP intermediary that forwards it to an HTTP/3 endpoint using Datagram Capsule. As this HTTP datagram usage is one that does not require to support of Capsule Datagram this endpoint is not setup to handle this Datagram capsule and discards it. 

So this can either be fixed in various ways, not only what this issue text suggests:
   1. requiring the Datagram capsule support for all HTTP datagram handling nodes. In other words change the first quote.
   2. Require the HTTP intermediary to re-encode any Datagram capsules to HTTP/3 datagram if the next hop is know to support it. i.e. make additional requirements on how HTTP Intermediaries act when forwarding.
   3. Forbid blind forwarding of HTTP datagram in HTTP intermediaries.

I think we should settle this part before going back to see how the text Mirja suggested changing matter. I think 1 and 2 are both working solutions, and would like to avoid 3. 

I think there is also a question on the implication of what it means to support HTTP datagram when one is an HTTP/3 endpoint or intermediary. Who is expected to support the Datagram capsule if the next node is not capable? 

So I think at the bottom this issue is really the question about the possibility to convert between HTTP/3 Datagram and Datagram capsule. I think we need to settle that question first. It is a question of what requirements one have on endpoints vs intermediaries. Lets start in that end.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: I actually think I prefer your option 3, caveated by saying "if you're an intermediary and you don't know the upgrade token, don't insert datagram capsules" . What concern do you have about option 3?

comments.author: gloinul
comments.body: Okay, I am skeptical against 3) on how it may make deployment of future extensions that require HTTP Datagram but doesn't need other than Intermediary forwarding. In that case deployment could be hampered if not all HTTP intermediaries are also HTTP/3 capable. It appears that using capsule protocol would be easier to enable over a legacy system. That might be a misconception from my part.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: @gloinul Thank you for clarifying, now I understand where the disconnect is. The draft currently says `Note that use of the Capsule Protocol is not required to use HTTP Datagrams` and you interpreted that as `Note that the Capsule Protocol is OPTIONAL to implement for implementations of HTTP Datagrams` but that's not what we intended, we meant `Note that it is possible for an HTTP extension to use HTTP Datagrams without using the Capsule Protocol`. I've written up #193 to remedy this

comments.author: gloinul
comments.body: @DavidSchinazi great that we managed to sort out what was the issue. As Lucas noted in the PR unless all HTTP Datagram implementation support and accept receiving Datagram capsule, even if not intended by the HTTP Extension, if unaware of HTTP extension transformation is allowed, it can fail. I think we need a bit more feedback on where people stand in this aspect.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: Thanks @gloinul. If the HTTP extension doesn't use capsules, then the implementation won't parse the data stream as capsules so there is no risk of accidentally receiving capsules. We added text to #193 to clarify the risks of not using the capsule protocol.

comments.author: mirjak
comments.body:
I think this was closed prematurely because the issue originally was about MUST or SHOULD and I don't think we concluded on this.

If the argument is that this is not enforceable, I think we should not use normatively language at all (and say something like "intermediaries are expected ..."). However, using SHOULD were we actually mean MUST, weakens the requirement and risk that this is misunderstood to be optional (while I think this is the core of the whole capsule protocol).

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: Reopening to discuss SHOULD vs MUST.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
I'd consider capsules to be similar to header fields (headers specifically, not trailers). Here's what HTTP says about them in https://httpwg.org/http-core/draft-ietf-httpbis-semantics-latest.html#rfc.section.5.1.p.6

>A proxy MUST forward unrecognized header fields unless the field name is listed in the [Connection](https://httpwg.org/http-core/draft-ietf-httpbis-semantics-latest.html#field.connection) header field ([Section 7.6.1](https://httpwg.org/http-core/draft-ietf-httpbis-semantics-latest.html#field.connection)) or the proxy is specifically configured to block, or otherwise transform, such fields. Other recipients SHOULD ignore unrecognized header and trailer fields. Adhering to these requirements allows HTTP's functionality to be extended without updating or removing deployed intermediaries.

Yeah, in actuality an intermediary can do lots of stuff, and in practice they do. But if a MUST is good enough for HTTP headers, why isn't it here?

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: From memory it was either @martinthomson or @ekr who cared strongly about this not being a MUST. I'm fine either way as long as we don't drag this one needlessly.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body:
To summarize the discussion on this issue up to this point:
* we're debating whether to tell intermediaries that they MUST or SHOULD forward unknown capsules unmodified
* implementors of intermediaries will not react to either one of these words differently
* endpoints have no way of enforcing this MUST
* some folks felt very strongly against MUST
* the working group landed on this design [a month ago](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/masque/GXaxmCJoo122ymqyAqTUaUFix_k/) and no new information has surfaced since

Based on the points above, there is no reason to hold up document progress based on a single word that will not have any impact. Therefore I'm closing this issue with no action.

issues.title: Interoperability for all HTTP Datagrams or defined by HTTP Extension
issues.author: gloinul
issues.body:
I think the draft do need to decide if it defines HTTP Datagrams to be always interoperable or if it is up to the HTTP extension to define how one becomes interoperable. As seen in #165 the later school of though might have been leading, while not considering the attempt to be generic. If one will leave it to the HTTP Extension, then I think a section is needed to make it clear what an HTTP Extension needs to think about and define to be interoperable. 

I would think making the basics of HTTP Datagrams interoperable including when Intermediaries are doing re-encoding without knowing the upgrade token might be the simplest even if it will require Datagram Capsule to be supported by all HTTP Extensions.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: What do you mean by "interoperable" here?

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: To add to my previous comment: I don't fully understand what this issue is about. HTTP Datagrams by themselves are interoperable but don't have semantics - they're a tool that HTTP extensions can use. The HTTP extensions interoperate between client and server implementation of such extension, and the intermediaries ferry bytes back and worth. Perhaps you could phrase this differently: what is the problem here? Is this document too vague such that it would be possible to write an HTTP extension that doesn't interoperate?

comments.author: gloinul
comments.body: Lets close this and take the discussion in #167

issues.title: HTTP content handling capability with Capsule protocol
issues.author: gloinul
issues.body:
I find the difference between HTTP 1.x and HTP/2 vs HTTP/3 when an endpoint support QUIC datagram quite worrying. So as capsules are sent instead of the message body in requests and response, for HTTP/3 when one have QUIC datagram support a method can be defined to use both the reliable body as well as HTTP datagrams. This is not possible over HTTP/3 when the QUIC stack doesn't support QUIC datagram or for HTTP 1.x or HTTP/2. I think this makes it very hard to define something that will just work. I Think the easy fix for this is to just define in addition to the Datagram capsule a body capsule that carries a fragment of the body, so that one can send over an upgraded path both parts of the body as well as the HTTP Datagrams. The fact that the Capsule protocol doesn't give feature parity even for HTTP/3 is deeply worrying in my view. 

I can understand how this has not come up prior as the existing HTTP methods that been targeted by this mechanism, i.e. Connect results in that the data stream becomes the capsule streams. However, if some other HTTP extension that using Extended Connect are used, then the need for both body and HTTP datagram could arise.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Successful CONNECT and extended CONNECT requests convert the request into a data stream, those bytes cease to be HTTP "content" (the term we should be using instead of "body"). 

Supporting HTTP content over capsules sounds like a sure-fire way to introduce security bugs. I don't see any reason to do that as part of this specification. Future extensions would need to do the security analysis and probably find that there's a better design to be had.

comments.author: gloinul
comments.body: Okay, but then I think the scope of this extension needs to be made clear to be limited to HTTP Extensions that has this semantics of converting the content.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
I don't think that is a hard scope though, and if it is, it is something we need to think hard about and come to consensus on.

Currently, if people find they really want to encode HTTP content in capsule, they are free to do so with all the risks that might entail. Being overly restrictive on future uses doesn't seem that helpful at this stage.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: +1 to what Lucas said, a future extension is free to design "HTTP content over capsules" if it needs it. We don't have a need for it today. The current scope is made clear by the text banning use of datagrams on requests that don't have known semantics for them

comments.author: gloinul
comments.body: I am fine with a clarification  that this support is currently not in scope due to reasons, and future HTTP extensions may be define additional capsule for content to enable this. I don't have a use cases, but currently HTTP/3 can support using both request content and HTTP datagrams simultanously.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: OK documenting that HTTP/3 is special, as a consideration for future specifications to be aware of, seems reasonable to me.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: +1. Marking this as editorial, we'll write up a PR to clarify that HTTP content can't be currently with capsules and that h3 is slightly special.

issues.title: Abstract: Unclear use of Both
issues.author: gloinul
issues.body:
In Abstract:

"Both are intended for use by HTTP extensions, not applications."

I think instead of using Both which is unclear, rather say HTTP Datagram and Capsule Protocol. That is at least what I interpret it to be in reference to.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: Agree, we should just write this out explicitly.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: SGTM

issues.title: Section 1: Reference of non-existing capabilities in websocket
issues.author: gloinul
issues.body:
Section 1:

`and unreliable delivery in WebSockets [RFC6455](or its successors).`

To my understanding WebSockets have no partial reliability features per that specification. So I think the formulation is missleading. To enable this in WebSockets, would it not require an update to WebSockets. I thought WebTrans is basically that update. So why not reference WebTrans here instead, it will anyway be an informational reference.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: These are examples of potential future extensions that serve to illustrate the motivation. The fact that we're not planning on building such examples does not diminish their usefulness. Readers might be more familiar with WebSocket than with WebTransport at this point.

issues.title: Introduction: Missmatching description of relation to HTTP or underlying transport.
issues.author: gloinul
issues.body:
Section 1.

"When the underlying transport protocol supports unreliable delivery (such as when the QUIC DATAGRAM extension is available in HTTP/3), they can use that capability."

"This document also describes the HTTP Capsule Protocol in Section 3, to allow conveyance of HTTP Datagrams when the QUIC DATAGRAM frame is unavailable or undesirable, such as when earlier versions of HTTP are in use."

To me there is a bit of mismatch between these two sentences and what HTTP/3 is prior to this extension.

The first indicate that datagram support is a capability of the underlying transport for the HTTP version but then link it hard to HTTP/3. While the HTTP/3 support is dependent on this extension in addition to a QUIC stack having Datagram support. While the second takes it as a property of the HTTP version, where it is assumed that earlier version can't support this, i.e. those that are defined to use TCP only. 

Technically a HTTP/3 endpoint with a QUIC stack without datagram support can  use capsules and this document does not require an endpoint to support QUIC datagram.

And the second statement should likely use a statement saying like …  unavailable or undesirable, such as when TCP is used as transport protocol as with HTTP/1.x and HTTP/2.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Fair point, HTTP 1 and 2 don't strictly require TCP either.

I think we can tweak these opening paragraphs a little to be more consistent and clear.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: SGTM

issues.title: Default endpoint behaviour of unknown capsule types
issues.author: mirjak
issues.body:
I don't think this was discussed previously in detail and the answer might just be no but would like to discuss this before we finally publish this spec.

There are two default behaviours specified:

- intermediaries should/must forward unknown capsule types unaltered, and
- endpoints must silently drop unknown capsule types.

The protocol would be more flexible if e.g. one could also instruct intermediates to drop and send an error instead, and if endpoints could be instructed to either drop silently or send an error. If any such behaviour would be useful, we need to define now e.g. by using two flags as part of the type field. Of course adding those flags would make the protocol also slightly more complicated. 

So just to be sure we do the right thing: are we sure we don't need to support this future flexibility and have selected the right default behaviour? Or are there any use cases where a different default behaviour would be required?

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Sending errors for unknown things doesn't really align with our attempts in HTTP land to avoid ossification in implementations (aka GREASING).

If there is some use of a capsule that needs acknowledgement it was received and/or processed, then that capsule should build the mechanism; be it either on a per-capsule basis or an upfront negotiation of capabilities before the capsule flow commences.

Our current error signaling mechanisms (stream or connection error) are terminal for a stream.. But I'm not seeing much value in trying to define an abstract error generation pattern just for capsules, without a concrete use case.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: @mirjak do you have an example of a use-case that would benefit from the erroring scheme? I'm not seeing any - it's more future-proof to drop at the endpoints and use new HTTP headers to indicate support for new capsules.

comments.author: mirjak
comments.body: If you negotiate all supported capsule types using http headers (or something else), isn't receiving an unknown capsulate type not automatically an error (and you should close the connection)?

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body: In my experience, closing connections in such cases is a way to build fragility into the deployment architecture, and achieves the opposite of the flexibility goal.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: Making this an error would also prevent sending capsules alongside the request. I really don't see the value of this proposed change.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body:
I'm proposing we close this issue with no action.

@mirjak if you have a specific use case that requires this new error scheme, then please share it.

comments.author: mirjak
comments.body:
My initial issue was about providing one or more flags to impact the handling of unknown capsule types. I already noted that this adds a bit of complexity but might provide higher flexibility for future extensions. I don't have a use case but wanted to trigger the discussion to ensure we didn't miss any use cases. Therefore I would like to keep this issue open a bit longer to see if more people have input or bring it to the list for discussion.

However, there is a second question here which is, if we don't have these flags, did we select the right default behaviour? For intermediaries I think the answer is clear, as the whole point of this protocol is to have a mechanism that can transverse an intermediary unaltered even if unknown to the intermediary (and there is a separate about having a MUST or SHOULD there, however that discussion has drifted a bit in a different direction). However, for the endpoint I'm not sure anymore we have chosen the right default behaviour. Currently the default is silent drop, however, as Lucas mentioned, an endpoint should never get into the situation where it receives an unknown capsule type as there always needs to be some negotiation that also defines the set of capsules that are supported. Therefore receiving an unknown capsule type is actually a protocol error and should probably treated similarly to all other protocol errors.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
> Currently the default is silent drop, however, as Lucas mentioned, an endpoint should never get into the situation where it receives an unknown capsule type as there always needs to be some negotiation that also defines the set of capsules that are supported. Therefore receiving an unknown capsule type is actually a protocol error and should probably treated similarly to all other protocol errors.

I'm not sure I meant to say that. 

If you're a receiving *endpoint*, you should be able to handle unknown capsules without error. That would allow someone to, for example, use the "connect-udp" token and extend it's behaviour via new capsule types that were not thought of at the time that "connect-udp" was invented. This is a property of HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 frames and streams already, and seems to me something we should emulate in capsule, we already define "reserved types for GREASING".

If we prevent unknown types unless prearranged, I can see that leading to a need for proliferation of e.g. upgrade tokens, which to my mind would not be a good way to design the system.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body:
+1 to Lucas: silent drop enables grease and new kinds of extensions.

Mirja: Happy to keep this issue around for the duration of the WGLC to see if anyone else has use-cases that benefit from this new error scheme.

comments.author: mirjak
comments.body: If we want this kind of additional extensibility, I think we should add a flag to have both options: just ignore or please tell me if you don't understand because otherwise we have to re-invent some kind of ACK scheme for each new type that we want to deploy this way.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: That flag can be added as a new extension. There's no use case for it so I don't see any reason to include in the base spec

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: Closing this since today marks the end of WGLC and we haven't seen any use cases for this proposed error scheme.

issues.title: Datagram related state is not well-defined
issues.author: DavidSchinazi
issues.body:
The draft currently states:
> HTTP/3 Datagrams MUST NOT be sent unless the corresponding stream's send side is open. Once the receive side of a stream is closed, incoming datagrams for this stream are no longer expected so related state can be released. State MAY be kept for a short time to account for reordering. Once the state is released, the received associated datagrams MUST be silently dropped.

However in PR #161, @mirjak points out that this "state" is not well defined. I agree, we should fix it.

Thinking about this more, I don't think we need the concept of related state. We can instead just say that received datagrams MUST be silently dropped if the stream receive side is closed.

comments.author: mirjak
comments.body:
I agree with removing the concept of state is better. I don't want to be overly nitty and the proposed sentence is better but there also nothing like "the stream receive side", as there can be multiple streams (open and closed), that's why I proposed

`If a datagram is received without associated state, the received datagrams MUST be silently dropped.`

Or if we don't want state, then it would be:

`If a datagram is received without an associated (open) stream, the received datagrams MUST be silently dropped.`

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body:
That's not quite right: there cannot be multiple streams, as datagrams are strongly associated with a client-initiated bidirectional stream. I'd phrase the paragraph as:

> HTTP/3 Datagrams MUST NOT be sent unless the corresponding stream's send side is
open. If a datagram is received after the receive side of the corresponding stream is closed,
the received datagrams MUST be silently dropped.

comments.author: mirjak
comments.body: That works. Thanks!

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: This answer is necessary because QUIC doesn't guarantee ordering, but is this necessarily true indefinitely?  But can I regard a datagram that arrives an hour after the stream closes as an error?

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: If you keep track of QUIC packet numbers, you can see that the peer closed the stream before it sent the datagram which means they violated a MUST. You're welcome to error if you detect that, but I don't think we should mandate this level of tracking.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: I'm not sure that that is a good strategy given how some deployments manage their packet numbers.  I'm talking about maybe running a really long timer.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: That introduces a way for an attacker to cause connection closure by delaying a specific packet. What problem are you trying to solve?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body: Good point.  I thought that we did similar in a few places in QUIC.  As you say, it's possible to enforce, but tricky.  The concern I'd have is that this effectively forbids enforcement, but maybe that's OK.

issues.title: 0-RTT and greater than or equal formulation for SETTINGS_H3_DATAGRAM
issues.author: gloinul
issues.body:
Section 2.2.1:

" When servers decide to accept
   0-RTT data, they MUST send a SETTINGS_H3_DATAGRAM setting greater
   than or equal to the value they sent to the client in the connection
   where they sent them the NewSessionTicket message."

As the SETTINGS_H3_DATAGRAM only allows value 0 or 1 is this just a way of
saying: Servers that accept 0-RTT data and have previously accepted HTTP Datagram and provide a session ticket MUST accept them for future connections referencing that ticket. ?

comments.body: Hi Magnus, I don't understand this editorial issue. Can you clarify what is unclear to you? In what way are you not understanding this paragraph?

comments.body:
@DavidSchinazi is my paraphrasing correct? 

If that is the case, I think the formulation is unnecessary convoluted and also hides an aspect. I reacted on the greater value for something that is only 0 or 1.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
The text seems precise enough to me. 
For the setting, 0 = off, 1 = on. You can't renage what you gave the client on a previous connection and go from 1 -> 0. But you can upgrade them and go from 0 => 1. Or you can send a setting with an identical value.

Since 1 is the maximum value defined by the setting, it seems trivial for a server to do the right thing with picking whether to send 0 or 1.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: @gloinul your paraphrasing is correct, though it's not precise enough for a normative requirement. Given that the current normative text is precise and unambiguous even if slightly convoluted I'm inclined to keep it as is. The fact that your paraphrasing was correct demonstrates that this text is clear enough.

comments.author: tfpauly
comments.body:
The longer form to be normatively correct would be something like this, I imagine:

> When clients use 0-RTT, they MAY store the value of the server's SETTINGS_H3_DATAGRAM setting. Doing so allows the client to send QUIC DATAGRAM frames in 0-RTT packets. When a server decides to accept 0-RTT data, it MUST send a SETTINGS_H3_DATAGRAM setting with a value of 1 if the previous value was 1 in the connection where it sent the client the NewSessionTicket message. If the previous value was 0, the server MAY send a value of either 0 or 1. If a client stores the value of the SETTINGS_H3_DATAGRAM setting with its 0-RTT state, it MUST validate that the new value of the SETTINGS_H3_DATAGRAM setting sent by the server in the handshake is 1 if the previous value was 1; if not, the client MUST terminate the connection with error H3_SETTINGS_ERROR. In all cases, the only two permitted value of the SETTINGS_H3_DATAGRAM setting parameter are 0 and 1.

I don't think that greatly improves the text, but it is a bit more explicit.

issues.title: Flow Control and Capsule/Datagram
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
This is a non-blocking comment from AD review. I have no concerns if the authors choose to close it with no action.

It might be worthwhile to discuss the interaction of stream flow control with capsule/datagram conversions. With other HTTP transactions, intermediaries can deliver whatever in-order bytes of the stream they have. When receiving capsules and emitting datagrams, if the stream flow control window is too small to accept the datagram size, there can be a deadlock. A sentence about this special case could avoid a silly implementer mistake.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
I think this goes beyond just intermediaries. Instead it applies to any consumer of capsules where they might be tempted to try and buffer the capsule, in the data stream, in its entirety before processing or consuming it. That might be obvious as a "bad thing" for implementers that are already used to handling H2 or H3 frames. However, you identify that the DATAGRAM capsule is particularly tempting to buffer because it should be handled atomically. 

So I think it might help to briefly point out some deadlock considerations about flow window sizes in relation to capsule sizes, and processing / release of further window credits.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: Adding a little bit of text to warn against such cases SGTM

issues.title: Error Handling section is sloppy with terms
issues.author: martinduke
issues.body:
In Sec 3.3:

When an error occurs in processing the Capsule Protocol, the receiver
   MUST treat the message as malformed or incomplete...

there are 2 other reference to malformed "messages" as a result of Capsule shenanigans.

but in the introduction it says that datagrams "are not part of message content". 

So what is "the message" that should be treated this way? I think you mean the Request or Response that initiated the Capsule protocol.

If that's correct, a more precise phrasing might be "MUST act as if the message that initiated the capsule protocol was malformed".

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Agree we can probably tighten things up here. 

For one, the definition of "data stream" in 3.1 presently says

> This specification defines the "data stream" of an HTTP request as the bidirectional stream of bytes that follows the header section of the request message and the final, successful (i.e., 2xx) response message.
> 
> In HTTP/1.x, the data stream consists of all bytes on the connection that follow the blank line that concludes either the request header section, or the response header section. As a result, only a single HTTP request starting the capsule protocol can be sent on HTTP/1.x connections.
> 
> In HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, the data stream of a given HTTP request consists of all bytes sent in DATA frames with the corresponding stream ID.

In isolation, this statement leaves it a little unclear whether trailing headers can appear after the data stream. In [7540bis section 8.5](https://httpwg.org/http2-spec/draft-ietf-httpbis-http2bis.html#section-8.5), that defines how CONNECT works, things are a lot clearer:

> Frame types other than [DATA](https://httpwg.org/http2-spec/draft-ietf-httpbis-http2bis.html#DATA) or stream management frames ([RST_STREAM](https://httpwg.org/http2-spec/draft-ietf-httpbis-http2bis.html#RST_STREAM), [WINDOW_UPDATE](https://httpwg.org/http2-spec/draft-ietf-httpbis-http2bis.html#WINDOW_UPDATE), and [PRIORITY](https://httpwg.org/http2-spec/draft-ietf-httpbis-http2bis.html#PRIORITY)) MUST NOT be sent on a connected stream and MUST be treated as a [stream error](https://httpwg.org/http2-spec/draft-ietf-httpbis-http2bis.html#StreamErrorHandler) ([Section 5.4.2](https://httpwg.org/http2-spec/draft-ietf-httpbis-http2bis.html#StreamErrorHandler)) if received.

My working assumption has been that data streams have similar requirements, but we don't explicitly state that anywhere, which is not great. If we tighten that up then it should become clearer that, once the capsule protocol is successfully negotiated, the HTTP message ended after the first HEADERS frames. We would still expect endpoints to apply some rules to frame processing on these data streams, and if there was a problem the data stream is malformed. Today we equate malformed data streams to malformed requests, and therefore delegate the handling of such problems (reset stream + error code) to the respect section in H2 or H3. I wonder actually if we should just state some explicit stream termination requirements. This does not change the actions that endpoint might take, but it does clarify the circumstances under which they should happen.

I'll prepare a PR for this to help illustrate my thinking.

To summarise:

1) If an endpoint screws up meeting the requirements of request or response field sections that bootstrap a capsule protocol instance, that is clearly a standard "malformed message"
2) If, after a capsule protocol instance has successully been created, an endpoint screws up anything on the data stream, that does not seem like a "malformed message"

comments.body: I can understand the impulse to avoid the term "stream" because then you're in the business of defining the behavior per HTTP version, but I'm sure you'll come up with some good language.

Hm, I think QPACK ended up perhaps too tightly coupled to HTTP semantics - at least it references Field Lines and Field Sections.  The specification itself is otherwise devoid of semantic meaning - it's just an encoding and compression scheme for name/value pairs.  I think it would be kind of a bummer if it couldn't be used, particularly by HTTP extensions, to convey compressed, structured metadata - like "middlers", etc.

But I can see @DavidSchinazi giving us a nudge to quit discussing QPACK here...
Oh I'm in complete agreement that HPACK/QPACK are very nice generic key-value compression schemes. It's slightly sad they are entwined with messages but that's what we've been dealt.

I'd rather define this once instead of having each method dictate what this contains. Binary would work too, text just felt simpler.

The issue there is that you would then need some sort of acknowledgement to know when your peer has parsed that frame. The unilateral model removes the need for acknowledgements at the HTTP level (for example HTTP/2 has an ACK bit on the SETTINGS frame for this reason).

I think something binary like Settings parameters has been too restrictive for extensibility. Depending exactly what extensibility people migh need, I think I'd probably still lean towards this being an encoded sf-list. This solves for many caveats of data-types and would give a nice pathway to migrate to binary Structured Fields if people really can't stomach strings in wire format.

> the sender of the frame unilateraly defines the semantics it will apply to the datagrams it
receives

This feels backwards to me - my inclination is to have the sender define the semantics of datagrams it will send on a flow ID.  This is similar to how unidirectional extension streams work -- the sender-chosen stream type identifies the semantics.

I don't think the analogy with stream types is correct. The semantics of stream types are determined by an IANA registry, whereas flow IDs are ephemeral per-connection numbers. If you reverse the direction then things break in the presence of reordering.

"I'm listening for X on Flow-ID Y" requires a roundtrip before the sender can even send.  Saying, "I'm sending you X on Flow-ID Y" doesn't break in the face of reordering, you just might lose some datagrams if your stack discards datagrams with unknown Flow IDs.  The receiver can also buffer datagrams on unknown Flow IDs for a while if it's concerned about this case.

Consider an extension for unreliable HTTP upload, where I send POST request headers on a stream and then the body comes in DATAGRAMs. If I've already seen the SETTINGS from the server and know it supports my extension, why do I need to wait another RTT to acquire a flow-ID?

pulls.title: Experiment with two layers of indirection
pulls.author: DavidSchinazi
pulls.body:
Similar to #37, this PR is a thought experiment aimed at seeing whether an alternate design makes sense. We're not planning on merging this as-is.

This design was inspired by a proposal by @bemasc. Ben gets the credit for the idea of using two layers of indirection here, and I take the blame for writing it down wrong.

Since this is really hard to review in PR form, I've uploaded an HTML version [here](https://davidschinazi.com/stuff/draft-ietf-masque-h3-datagram.html) so I definitely suggest reading that instead.

Conceptually, I think this proposal is easier to reason about, and it has the advantage of requiring minimal work from intermediaries. Its downside is that the wire format is slightly less efficient because it requires another varint to be sent per datagram, but I think we can live with that.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
I'm still digesting this proposal, so take the following comments with a pinch of salt.

I think the PR description glosses over some design changes and buries the lede. The major changes in this proposal seems to be that Flow IDs are no longer connection global, and Flow ID usage negotitation is no longer based on headers. If I were to reword the proposed concepts based on my understanding, we're talking about flow groups bound to each request. Flows can be added to the group during its lifetime but never retired. A flow allocation service needs only ensure uniqueness of flow IDs in a flow group. I'm failing to see why it is better to have an identifying tuple (stream-id:flow-id) instead of a global identifier (flow-id) but happy to be pointed out to why.

The examples are helpful so thanks for putting those in (I might have opinions on actually keeping them but this spec is currently weaker for not including any, I think we tracked this on a ticket already.)

If I were to summarise my understanding, this proposal replaces

```
HEADERS (on stream 44) {
  method: CONNECT-UDP
  {other headers}
  datagram-flow-id: 0
}
```

with 

```
HEADERS (on stream 44) {
  method: CONNECT-UDP
  {other headers}
}

RELIABLE_DATAGRAM (on stream 44) { 
  Flow-ID: 0
  Registered-Flow-Id: 1
  Extension-String: ""
}
```

The claim is that this makes it easier to reason about things, but frankly at this stage I can see it making some things harder. No longer can a MASQUE server reason about creating a tunnel based on HEADERS alone, it needs to combine that with some additional information that is delivered on the request stream but is not part of an HTTP request semantic. Such is the nature of H2/H3 frames, but I find it odd that the flow ID is described as an end-to-end signal in the same breath as being described as bound to a request context.

The surprising change I find in this design is it makes the flow registration unreliable, with a very weak suggestion to use something reliable. Can you embelish on why you picked this direction?  I'm not convinced if we want to do this flow groups thing but if we did, I find the overloading of RELIABLE_DATAGRAM unhelpful. It seems that you could combine some of this proposal with the REGISTER_DATAGRAM_FLOW_ID from #37. That would provide a clearer separation between the datagram control plane and data plane. One advantage of using a frame delivered on the request stream is that it avoids Flow-ID 0 being special case, which is ugly because it prevents requets from being made on Stream-ID 0. Another advantage is that it allows strict ordering of frames, in case we wanted to add rules about in-order flow ID usage.

Finally, I'm slightly confused by how the CONNECT-IP example would work in reality if the server did not support the `"ip=192.0.2.42,port=443"` extension. If it drops the DATAGRAM payload silently, that seems like a sad move. I think someone (maybe Alan?) suggested somewhere that a frame-based registration design could benefit from some control-plane signal. I'm beginning to lean toward some further types of controls for flows, like an H3-layer STOP_SENDING/RESET_FLOW.

To to conclude my understanding/opinion of this proposal

1. flow IDs are request-scoped, not global. I'm not sure if this is a good, bad or neutral change.
1. flow IDs reservation is  done using a frame and can be done during the lifetime of a request
  * This makes things gnarlier for my current implementation. It would require API changes to expose such events to an application.
1. flow ID reservation could include extension strings I don't understand. If so, I have to just drop all datagrams for that flow and can't signal it back to my peer.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
Hi Lucas,

>No longer can a MASQUE server reason about creating a tunnel based on HEADERS alone, it needs to combine that with some additional information that is delivered on the request stream but is not part of an HTTP request semantic.

I'm not sure what you mean by "creating a tunnel", but note that the actual call to `bind()`, to allocate a UDP socket, can indeed be performed based on the headers alone.  (Actually, you don't even need the headers.)

It's true that, like #37, this proposal allows flows to be created at any time during CONNECT-UDP's lifetime.  This feature is not strictly necessary, but can be useful in various scenarios.  For example, it is hard to imagine how QUIC connection ID compression can work without this.

> Such is the nature of H2/H3 frames, but I find it odd that the flow ID is described as an end-to-end signal in the same breath as being described as bound to a request context.

HTTP requests are end-to-end: they are communicated through the intermediaries but are not _for_ the intermediaries.  They're not even version-specific.  Flows in MASQUE have these properties too.

> The surprising change I find in this design is it makes the flow registration unreliable, with a very weak suggestion to use something reliable. Can you embelish on why you picked this direction?

I interpreted this as "you definitely want to use reliable registration, but technically nobody is going to enforce this requirement on you".  I think we can adjust this easily enough.

> I'm not convinced if we want to do this flow groups thing but if we did, I find the overloading of RELIABLE_DATAGRAM unhelpful. It seems that you could combine some of this proposal with the REGISTER_DATAGRAM_FLOW_ID from #37. That would provide a clearer separation between the datagram control plane and data plane.

The key claim of this design is that flows are only meaningful end-to-end, so exposing them to intermediaries is unnecessary.  From the HTTP transport's perspective, a flow-registration is just more data to be routed along with the request/response; it's only meaningful to the client and server.

> One advantage of using a frame delivered on the request stream is that it avoids Flow-ID 0 being special case, which is ugly because it prevents requets from being made on Stream-ID 0.

FWIW, I think "zero is special" is a fairly elegant common pattern.

> Another advantage is that it allows strict ordering of frames, in case we wanted to add rules about in-order flow ID usage.

It's not spelled out here, but RELIABLE_DATAGRAMs would be strictly ordered, so this is still possible.

> Finally, I'm slightly confused by how the CONNECT-IP example would work in reality if the server did not support the `"ip=192.0.2.42,port=443"` extension.

I think @DavidSchinazi is implying that the listed extensions all happen to be Mandatory To Implement for the corresponding methods.  I agree, it would be good to discuss how non-mandatory extensions are negotiated.

> I'm beginning to lean toward some further types of controls for flows, like an H3-layer STOP_SENDING/RESET_FLOW.

This is a key advantage of the two-layer design here.  These types of commands are only meaningful end-to-end, but without the second layer, adding new commands requires upgrading every intermediary and negotiating support in SETTINGS at each hop.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:
Hey Ben, 

Thanks for the reply, it paints a much fuller picture. I'm still wondering how this form of design might work across HTTP/1, 2 and 3 but that is a broader question for the WG so I'll leave aside. I'm not sure how best to reply here but I'll give quoting a shot. 

> I'm not sure what you mean by "creating a tunnel", but note that the actual call to bind(), to allocate a UDP socket, can indeed be performed based on the headers alone. (Actually, you don't even need the headers.)

As my first comment, I probably had the weakest view of the proposal. Based on the current design, a MASQUE server could reject a request if, for example, it detected a bad flow ID. I realize now that some of those failure conditions just go away. So I retract my comment.

> It's true that, like #37, this proposal allows flows to be created at any time during CONNECT-UDP's lifetime. This feature is not strictly necessary, but can be useful in various scenarios. For example, it is hard to imagine how QUIC connection ID compression can work without this.

Yep this seems like a useful extension point and something that is difficult to achieve today.

> >     The surprising change I find in this design is it makes the flow registration unreliable, with a very weak suggestion to use something reliable. Can you embelish on why you picked this direction?

> I interpreted this as "you definitely want to use reliable registration, but technically nobody is going to enforce this requirement on you". I think we can adjust this easily enough.

Why not enforce it though? What scenario benefits from an unreliable flow creation. DATAGRAMs can be lost in the network or in the application buffers. The opportunity for problems get worse when adding intermediaries.

> The key claim of this design is that flows are only meaningful end-to-end, so exposing them to intermediaries is unnecessary. From the HTTP transport's perspective, a flow-registration is just more data to be routed along with the request/response; it's only meaningful to the client and server.

That explanation helps, thanks. I think this speaks to my earlier point though. It seems this is a design that adds stuff to HTTP message but is not HTTP metadata or HTTP content. So what is it? H2 and H3 frames are hop-by-hop but their contents can be forwarded without being processed by anyone but the intended recipient. An intermediary that knows how to forward a request can forward frame contents. It seems this is the desired goal of using RELIABLE_DATAGRAM for control and data planes. But my point is that you could equally define REGISTER_DATAGRAM_FLOW_ID and other control frames that behave similarly, without having to overload them as a DATAGRAM on a special flow.

> FWIW, I think "zero is special" is a fairly elegant common pattern.

We avoided it for QUIC and HTTP/3. If every deployment of HTTP/3 DATAGRAM would have to burn the first request stream, that seems ugly to me.

>>    Finally, I'm slightly confused by how the CONNECT-IP example would work in reality if the server did not support the "ip=192.0.2.42,port=443" extension.

comments.body:
> > > ```
> > > The surprising change I find in this design is it makes the flow registration unreliable, with a very weak suggestion to use something reliable. Can you embelish on why you picked this direction?
> > > ```
> 
> > I interpreted this as "you definitely want to use reliable registration, but technically nobody is going to enforce this requirement on you". I think we can adjust this easily enough.

> Why not enforce it though?

I'm fine with enforcing it, so long as we're clear that enforcement only happens at the endpoints.  Intermediaries shouldn't be looking past the Quarter Stream ID.

> > The key claim of this design is that flows are only meaningful end-to-end, so exposing them to intermediaries is unnecessary. From the HTTP transport's perspective, a flow-registration is just more data to be routed along with the request/response; it's only meaningful to the client and server.
> 
> That explanation helps, thanks. I think this speaks to my earlier point though. It seems this is a design that adds stuff to HTTP message but is not HTTP metadata or HTTP content. So what is it?

In an idealized version of HTTP, I see a stack of layers: hop, cache, exchange (request/response, end-to-end), method, resource (payload/representation).  The Quarter Stream ID is part of the hop layer.  Everything past that point is owned by the exchange.  The Flow ID, commands, and extension types are at the method layer.  The content of the extensions is at the resource layer.

Concretely, this means that intermediaries can forward datagrams for unrecognized methods, even if we cannot predict what requirements future methods may have for datagrams.

> H2 and H3 frames are hop-by-hop but their contents can be forwarded without being processed by anyone but the intended recipient.

Yes, and this PR essentially defines a frame type that means "forward this without processing unless you're the intended recipient".

> An intermediary that knows how to forward a request can forward frame contents. It seems this is the desired goal of using RELIABLE_DATAGRAM for control and data planes. But my point is that you could equally define REGISTER_DATAGRAM_FLOW_ID and other control frames that behave similarly, without having to overload them as a DATAGRAM on a special flow.
> 
> > FWIW, I think "zero is special" is a fairly elegant common pattern.
> 
> We avoided it for QUIC and HTTP/3. If every deployment of HTTP/3 DATAGRAM would have to burn the first request stream, that seems ugly to me.

The obvious alternative is to put a DatagramType varint after the Quarter Stream ID, like an H3 frame on a stream.  This costs us one byte of MTU.  I don't think it buys us anything concrete, but I'm willing to spend a byte if it makes the design feel more consistent.

> > > I'm beginning to lean toward some further types of controls for flows, like an H3-layer STOP_SENDING/RESET_FLOW.
> 
> > This is a key advantage of the two-layer design here. These types of commands are only meaningful end-to-end, but without the second layer, adding new commands requires upgrading every intermediary and negotiating support in SETTINGS at each hop.
> 
> I see two separate things. First, it is useful to be able to handle DATAGRAM frames with different formats, without needing all points in the change to understand how to process that format - I agree with this. Second, we can use DATAGRAM frames to carry control messages for managing datagram flows. This one I have more of a problem with, how extensible does flow management need to be? For this proposal, changes are needed to add RELIABLE_DATAGRAM support through the chain in the first instance. Adding support for other frames at the same time doesn't much more difficult.

Exposing the concept of flows to intermediaries makes them everything much more complicated.  For example, intermediaries would need their own flow count limits to avoid memory exhaustion.  Will clients and servers be able to figure out what happened when that limit is reached?  In the case of flow cleanup commands, the commands would presumably need to be ack'd end-to-end before flows could be reused, and both the commands and the acks would need to be interpreted and translated by intermediaries.  As an intermediary, what do I do with a datagram on a mapping for which a "stop" command has been forwarded but the "ack" has not yet been observed?  This complexity is not buying us anything.

Extensibility, with additional commands negotiated via SETTINGS, is even more of a mess.  If I'm a CDN reverse proxy for myriad backends with different capabilities, what commands do I claim to support?

I think we're much better off if we can draw a clear, simple line between hop-by-hop and end-to-end data.

There's a bit of contradiction here.  You claim that capsules are end-to-end; yet stream resets are per-hop mechanism, and in general I don't believe there is a reliable error propagation of stream reset codes across hops.

As far as I know, HTTP/3 doesn't have any other way to abruptly close request streams apart from reseting the stream. That reset will be propagated, and if the error code is changed that's not a big deal. This matches how HTTP/3 CONNECT reacts to a TCP RST for example.

You could use a header, but if you've already defined an extension key for the multiple context use-case, why have to define a header too? I prefer the simplicity and symmetry of using the same mechanism.

It's good behaviour to propagate errors across hops, even if they require mapping. For example, see the H2-H3 mapping advice in https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-quic-http-34#appendix-A.4.1.

I think the text is fine right to focus on HTTP/3 right now. Subsequent follow up work to make this design work over other HTTP versions can add guidance on how to propagate errors if specific advice is needed. I wouldn't worry about it in isolation since we might overlook details.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body:
@afrind you're the one who asked for this :-)

The benefit of a semi-opaque capsule is that it allows defining new capsules without having to update every single intermediary in the chain, because intermediaries forward all unknown capsules.

Non-opqaue (transparent?) CAPSULEs are not forwarded in their unmodified entirety.  

Should we state here that there are two types of CAPSULE (opaque and transparent)?.  Opaque CAPSULEs are always forwarded in their unmodified entirety.  Transparent CAPSULEs may be inspected and decapsulated by an intermediary and forwarded via a semantically equivalent protocol construct, when available.

Also in this PR, the DATAGRAM CAPSULE is *not* reliable end-to-end (see line 198), since converting to an H3 datagram on any hop along the path makes it unreliable.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
> Is there something implied here about how the intermediary will pack DATAGRAM frames into QUIC packets?

The implication here is that the intermediary (1) knows a lower bound on the QUIC MTU and (2) never adds frames to a packet that is already larger than this bound (if it allows such packets at all).  I believe this is always true for QUIC, although I'm not sure it's stated explicitly anywhere.

comments.author: DavidSchinazi
comments.body: @bemasc can you clarify what you meant by "a lower bound on the QUIC MTU" ? The MTU can change dynamically due to changes outside of QUIC's control so the only real lower bound is 1200 - and we need to be able to send packets larger than that.

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body: I mean that, at any given time, a QUIC endpoint has a lower bound L on the estimated path MTU.  This lower bound is sometimes wrong, but it's never zero.  If an H3 DATAGRAM produces a QUIC packet that is larger than L, we just need to be sure that QUIC won't add other frames to this packet.  (I don't know if QUIC will send this packet or just drop the datagram, but either way, DPLPMTUD on the inner connection will work fine.)

```
           hop 1              hop 2                 hop 3
Client  -->   Intermediary A  -->   Intermediary B  --> Target
```

For hop2, which is QUIC, it must have a minimum PMTU of 1200. The maximum PMTU could be bigger. The maximum QUIC packet size that can be sent should be the min(max MTU, max_udp_payload_size advertised by peer). After the intermediary gets the H3 DATAGRAM payload, it will need to reencode it. We're suggesting into a QUIC DATAGRAM frame, with H3 DATAGRAM headers. This reencoding could have different overhead sizes (hop2 might have larger QUIC packet overheads, or H3 DATAGRAM overheads.

Is the suggestion that the intermediary is using a PMTU size P1, and if it sees a H3 DATAGRAM that would produce a packet larger that P1, it should try to send it as a sort of probe?

comments.author: bemasc
comments.body:
> This reencoding could have different overhead sizes (hop2 might have larger QUIC packet overheads, or H3 DATAGRAM overheads.

That's fine, so long as the overhead of each hop rarely changes.

> Is the suggestion that the intermediary is using a PMTU size P1, and if it sees a H3 DATAGRAM that would produce a packet larger that P1, it should try to send it as a sort of probe?

It could try to send it, or it could drop it.  (It's not much of a "probe", since the intermediary won't necessarily know if it was dropped.)  Either way, the end-to-end DPLPMTUD will converge to some working value, which is all that matters.

comments.author: LPardue
comments.body:

Longer term, I think what we'll probably end up with is a whole section that collects intermediary concerns. But until we arrive at that point, a better way to present the matter at hand could be something like the following, which is intended to follow on the theme of discussion from the paragraphs in that section.

"Intermediaries that receive HTTP Datagrams in QUIC DATAGRAM frames need to decide how to forward them. If the onward connection supports QUIC DATAGRAM frames, intermediaries SHOULD attempt to forward HTTP Datagrams in a QUIC frame. pulls.title: Make datagram contexts optional to implement
pulls.author: DavidSchinazi
pulls.body:
[WebTransport](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-webtrans-http3) uses HTTP Datagrams but doesn't currently have a need for datagram contexts. Because of this, some members of the WebTransport community prefer to not have to implement datagram contexts. This PR changes how datagram contexts are negotiated to make them optional to implement. One important design goal of this change was to allow optimistic use of contexts: in other words, the client shouldn't have to wait a round trip to find out whether contexts are supported before being able to optimistically use them.

Before this PR, contexts were mandatory to implement and the client would decide whether to use them by sending either REGISTER_DATAGRAM_CONTEXT or REGISTER_DATAGRAM_NO_CONTEXT.

With this PR, endpoints use a new Sec-Use-Datagram-Contexts header to indicate support. The PR makes a few small tweaks to capsules in order to allow the optimistic use described above. In particular, it incorporates the DATAGRAM capsule split from #82 as that allows the client to use contexts before knowing whether the server supports them because the server can just drop the variant of the capsule with contexts.

[Rendered view of this PR here](https://ietf-wg-masque.github.io/draft-ietf-masque-h3-datagram/context_impl_optional/draft-ietf-masque-h3-datagram.html).

pulls.title: Simplify by removing formats and registration
pulls.author: tfpauly
pulls.body:
- Remove datagram format registry -- new capsule types can be used instead
- Delegate context ID registration to methods/protocols, which can define new capsule types
- Remove the need for header negotiation to support contexts. Individual methods can define their own headers for negotiation.
- Datagram contexts don't always need to be used, but there's an implicit "context 0" which has a format that must be defined by each method. The presence of a context ID in a datagram is encoded in the "encoded stream ID".

High level comments: 

Do we need to be as generic about transparent and opaque now?  Perhaps we can strictly state how an intermediary can convert between native DATAGRAMs and Datagram Capsules in both directions, and must forward any other capsules unmodified unless otherwise specified in a capsule's definition.

If we are baking the Datagram Capsule into The Capsule Protocol (TCP - sorry, couldn't resist) with a code point in this document, then is it safe to say that the intended usage is for conveying datagrams and optional request related information over a request stream? ```suggestion

You already say "encoded stream identifier" and the goal is to associate with request streams.  In WebTransport, we might use those bidirectional streams without making them requests, which will require (or at least allow) some additional checking to see that the identified stream contains a request, but that's something WebTransport can handle.

There is text missing from the introduction here that establishes the conditions on the use of capsule protocol.  That is, it only applies to those protocols that use extended CONNECT and also opt in to the use of the capsule protocol.

The nice thing with the draft up until this point is that it doesn't constrain the use of datagrams to those protocols that use extended CONNECT.  This part does.

(I know that this is perhaps fanciful, but I can imagine uses for regular HTTP requests that are enhanced by the use of DATAGRAM frames.)
This bit belongs up front.

👍

I might amend this to include the condition that the intermediary understand the semantics of the request enough to know that capsules are in use:

```suggestion
Capsules MUST be forwarded unmodified by intermediaries, with the exception of
the DATAGRAM capsule. An intermediary that understands the request semantics 
sufficient to know that capsules are in use MAY parse, add, or remove DATAGRAM
capsules; see {{datagram-capsule}}. Definitions of new Capsule Types MAY specify
custom intermediary processing.
```

What I don't want to see is intermediaries guessing that a particular unknown `:protocol` is using capsules when they do not.  Splicing in DATAGRAM frames/capsules in that context might go badly wrong.

> A server MUST NOT send any Transfer-Encoding or Content-Length header fields in a 2xx (Successful) response. If a client receives a Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding header fields in a successful response, it MUST treat that response as malformed.

1. the capsule protocol is not in use for a response unless it includes a 2xx status code
2. the capsule protocol MUST NOT be used with messages that contain Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding

> A request message does not have content.

There are cases where Content-Length can be zero, but that is limited, not universal.  It's only CONNECT that gets that special handling.  For a new method, the capsule protocol will need to be used for the request body, which means that the request will have content.

> A successful response message does not have content.

Again, this is not going to be the case for anything other than CONNECT.

In particular, I need that extension to work without costing a round trip (what I've been calling "zero-latency extensibility"). Let me go into more detail as to why RELIABLE_DATAGRAM is important to that.

The datagram context extension works as follows: it is negotiated by adding a header to both request and response, and when both endpoints support it, it adds a context ID varint at the start of the HTTP Datagram Payload field.

Now, in order to achieve zero-latency extensibility, the client needs to be able to send datagrams before receiving the server headers in such a way that the server can correctly parse them (if you add the context ID and the server doesn't support the extension, you don't want the server to parse the context ID as part of the payload).

So here's my idea for how to accomplish that. The extension says the following:
- clients that support the extension are not allowed to send QUIC DATAGRAM frames nor DATAGRAM capsule before they've received the server headers
- the extension defines a new RELIABLE_DATAGRAM_EXT capsule that can be sent before and after receiving server headers
```
Extended Reliable Datagram Capsule {
  Type (i) = RELIABLE_DATAGRAM_EXT,
  Length (i),
  Context ID (i),
  HTTP Datagram Payload (..),
}
```
- the extension does not change the semantics of the RELIABLE_DATAGRAM capsule, that still does not contain a Context ID
```
Reliable Datagram Capsule {
  Type (i) = RELIABLE_DATAGRAM,
  Length (i),
  HTTP Datagram Payload (..),
}
```
- when both endpoints support the extension (after receiving headers) the extension changes the semantics of both the QUIC DATAGRAM frame and DATAGRAM capsule to include a Context ID at the start:
```
Datagram Capsule {
  Type (i) = DATAGRAM,
  Length (i),
  Context ID (i),
  HTTP Datagram Payload (..),
}
HTTP/3 Datagram { // contents of QUIC DATAGRAM frame
  Quarter Stream ID (i),
  Context ID (i),
  HTTP Datagram Payload (..),
}
```
- if the client wishes to use zero-latency extensibility, it can send RELIABLE_DATAGRAM and RELIABLE_DATAGRAM_EXT before receiving the server headers. Both of these will be parsed correctly by servers, whether or not the server supports the extension.

All of this relies on the fact that there is one bit that differentiates the DATAGRAM capsule from the RELIABLE_DATAGRAM capsule (the bit is in the capsule type), so that the extension can give the two capsules different semantics in a way that is backwards compatible.

What I like about this design is that the added complexity to the HTTP Datagram spec is as minimal as possible: it just requires two case statements instead of one in the switch statement that parses capsule types.

I'm OK removing the RELIABLE_DATAGRAM capsule from this PR, as long as we have some other mechanism that I can use to write my extension.

1. A client that supports an extension can try to use the extension before receiving confirmation that the server supports it

But how would an extended server handle a non-extended client in that case? The way this process is supposed to work is that *this* PR is supposed to include the points on which we had consensus, and that means when people object to things which clearly don't, they are removed and deferred for later discussion. If that's not going to happen, then we can just abandon this PR and go back to real time discussion.

> A different issue that I'd like to raise (although I can live with this) is that I'm not really a fan of the extension-that-changes-the-semantics-of-DATAGRAM scheme that is being proposed here.

I am inclined to agree, but I see the solution as moving the demux higher in the protocol stack (eg: to CONNECT-UDP or CONNECT-IP) rather than down (into QUIC or H3 Datagram).  CONNECT-IP can say all DATAGRAMs on a CONNECT-IP stream have a specific format after the stream ID that includes "Context ID", "Format Type", etc, and this doesn't need to be negotiated at all.  I'd slightly prefer if those protocols used less generic concepts in doing so, but can live with it either way.

> the issue there is that it doesn't allow the client to send an unextended datagram in its first flight.

I assume you mean 'unextended DATAGRAM Capsule'.  In that case, I think I understand, which is that a DATAGRAM Capsule can be converted to a QUIC DATAGRAM by an intermediary, and there's ambiguity at a server that supports the extension after it confirms support: when did the client receive confirmation and start sending extended QUIC DATAGRAMs?

The client can still send DATAGRAM Capsules in this case, and move to QUIC DATAGRAM after it knows whether the server supports the extension or not.  Is there a real use case for sending both extended and non-extended DATAGRAMs in 0-RTT, where we're willing to sacrifice HoL blocking resilience and possible flow control constraints for the extended ones, but not willing to do so for the non-extended ones?  Or maybe the use-cases are small but we think the cost of RELIABLE_DATAGRAM is low and maybe has other utility?

This brings me back here:

> I'm not really a fan of the extension-that-changes-the-semantics-of-DATAGRAM scheme that is being proposed here.

I think we've shown that it's pretty hard to negotiate changes to QUIC DATAGRAM formats on the fly.  Let's not do that.  The cost of easy extensibility is an additional byte (or two) of header information inside the datagram payload of protocols that need it.  If CONNECT-UDP needs to have a such a header I can live with that.

QUIC DATAGRAM frames and DATAGRAM capsules need to have the exact same semantics, because intermediaries convert blindly between them so you can't know how they were originally sent. That's why my proposal forbids sending either when you support the extension and haven't yet received the peer's headers.

My personal opinion is that
- the cost of having RELIABLE_DATAGRAM for an implementation that doesn't care is very low
- RELIABLE_DATAGRAM has value in and of itself
- moving the complexity of contexts to their own extension allows defining different ways to do this down the road, whereas if we say that CONNECT-UDP starts with a varint we've committed to this context design forever

The HTTP WG is working on a style guide, see https://github.com/httpwg/admin/blob/main/style-guide.md

In line with the style, the reference to structured fields is updated in #147 because it's less contentious. What remains here is probably more so.

First, move the consideration for intermediaries to the bottom of the section. It doesn't seem a leading item to me. 

Then we start the section with a  focus on defining the field itself. The ABNF is probably the bit we'll disagree with. It seems in trying to be specific on the Item type, you've written out the the subcomponents of the ABNF. This is something that is being discussed in the HTTP WG list. Personally I don't like being overly specific in the ABNF because it could be misconstrued as something that is SF-like but not really SF. As far as a generic SF parser goes, it will only validate that the thing is an Item and it will be up to higher layers to apply additional constraints on that. Parameters can always appear with an Item on the wire, whether an application allows that or not is a different matter. Restating ABNF makes this topic more thorny.

When QUIC Datagrams are unavailable or undesirable, HTTP Datagrams can be sent

In {{datagrams}}, this document describes HTTP Datagrams, a convention that
supports the bidirectional and possibly multiplexed exchange of data inside an HTTP

part of message content; instead, they are intended for use by HTTP extensions (such as the CONNECT
```

type (including a List, such as when multiple field lines are sent) MUST be handled as if the field were not present by recipients. This
```

It might be better to NOT focus on upgrade tokens so much as the primary mechanism here and below; after all, they're just identifiers.

```
